speaker: GUIDE
text: The last chapter ended with a man and a woman naked and unashamed in a good garden. This chapter answers the question every reader eventually asks: if the world began like that, why is it like this?

speaker: READER
text: Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’”

speaker: GUIDE
text: The chapter opens with a pun English cannot keep. The pair were naked, arummim. The serpent is crafty, arum. The two words sound almost the same.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The ancient world wove the snake into its royal and sacred imagery. Genesis calls it simply a creature the LORD God had made. But later Scripture names the enemy behind the voice:

speaker: READER
text: that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan

speaker: GUIDE
text: He never commands. He only asks, and his first move is a question about what God said.

speaker: READER
text: The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden,

speaker: READER
text: but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, ‘You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.’”

speaker: GUIDE
text: God gave every tree freely and set one limit. She drops the freely, adds touching, and softens the warning. She shrinks the gift and enlarges the limit.

speaker: READER
text: “You will not surely die,” the serpent told the woman.

speaker: READER
text: “For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: The serpent takes God's own warning and puts a not in front of it. He contradicts God word for word, and paints the Giver of every tree as jealous. The root of sin, as Genesis tells it, is not ignorance but distrust.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Notice too that the narrator says the LORD God, His covenant name, but in this conversation they say only God. The personal name drops out just as trust in Him is dissolving.

speaker: READER
text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.

speaker: GUIDE
text: This is the only window the narrator gives into her mind, and it climbs. Good for food: the appetite. Pleasing to the eyes: the eye. Desirable for wisdom: ambition.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Desirable is the verb of the tenth commandment, you shall not covet. What God made to be enjoyed becomes something to be seized. And the man was with her, saying nothing at all.

speaker: READER
text: And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Their eyes are opened, but what they see is their own exposure. One act fractures every relationship at once, and shame arrives before any sentence is spoken. The fig leaves are their own attempt to cover it.

speaker: READER
text: Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Walking is the verb later used for God's presence moving through Israel's camp. And they hide from Him among the very trees He planted.

speaker: READER
text: But the LORD God called out to the man,

speaker: GOD
text: “Where are you?”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Many readers see this question at the centre of the chapter. The turning point is not the eating but the God who comes looking. He knows where they are. He asks so that the guilty will speak the truth.

speaker: READER
text: “I heard Your voice in the garden,” he replied, “and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GOD
text: “Who told you that you were naked?”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: READER
text: asked the LORD God.

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GOD
text: “Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: READER
text: And the man answered, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GUIDE
text: The man said nothing until he was questioned, and now he speaks to excuse himself.

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: READER
text: Then the LORD God said to the woman,

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GOD
text: “What is this you have done?”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: READER
text: “The serpent deceived me,” she replied, “and I ate.”

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GUIDE
text: The sin travelled from serpent to woman to man. The blame is passed back down the line. What she says is true, but it is not a defence.

chapter: The woman whom You gave me
speaker: GUIDE
text: And God questions the man and the woman, but puts no question to the serpent. He does not negotiate with evil. He sentences it.

speaker: READER
text: So the LORD God said to the serpent:

speaker: GOD
text: “Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and every beast of the field! On your belly will you go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Cursed falls on the serpent, and on the ground, never on the man or the woman themselves. Even in Isaiah's renewed world, this one sentence stands:

speaker: READER
text: the food of the serpent will be dust

speaker: GOD
text: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Enmity means open war. The rescue of the world begins as God's declaration of war on evil.

speaker: GUIDE
text: One verb stands behind both blows: the head against the heel, a fatal blow against a wounding one. And the seed is he. A long war between two lines, but the decisive blow is struck by one.

speaker: GUIDE
text: This is the first announcement of the gospel, spoken before a single sentence falls on the man and the woman.

speaker: READER
text: To the woman He said:

speaker: GOD
text: “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth; in pain you will bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Her pain is the same word as the man's toil. And the desire and the rule describe a marriage bent by sin, not God's design: a sorrowful description of the world under judgment, never a charter for it.

speaker: READER
text: And to Adam He said:

speaker: GOD
text: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.

speaker: GOD
text: Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.

speaker: GOD
text: By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground, because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Chapter two ran from dust to a living man. Chapter three runs that film backward: the man taken from the ground will return to it.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Yet mercy is laced through the judgment. Childbearing continues, so the promised seed can still come. Work continues, so life goes on.

speaker: READER
text: And Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Eve sounds like the Hebrew for living. In the very hour death enters, a small act of hope in God's promise.

speaker: READER
text: And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The fig leaves were their own covering. These garments are God's, and the words are the ones used when Moses clothed Israel's priests.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The text does not describe a sacrifice, so the link is an inference, but a fair one: the covering came from a life taken.

speaker: READER
text: Then the LORD God said,

speaker: GOD
text: “Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever...”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Even the exile is a mercy. It guards them from living forever in a fallen state.

speaker: READER
text: Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.

speaker: READER
text: So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.

speaker: GUIDE
text: To Israel this sounded like being barred from the sanctuary: its door faced east, and cherubim were worked into the veil before the Most Holy Place.

speaker: GUIDE
text: And east becomes a direction in Genesis. Cain settles east of Eden. Babel's builders journey east. Humanity keeps moving away from the presence it lost.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Verse fifteen does not name the victor. The promise narrows to Abraham, then to David, and comes to rest on one person. God sent His Son, Paul says,

speaker: READER
text: born of a woman

speaker: GUIDE
text: Luke traces Jesus back to Adam, and the next scene is the temptation. The last Adam meets the same enemy in a wilderness, hungry, and answers with what God said. He wins where the first man lost.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Adam hid among the trees. Christ was hung on a tree. Adam reached for what was forbidden. Christ, in a garden, prayed:

speaker: READER
text: not as I will, but as You will

speaker: GUIDE
text: Adam wore thorns as the fruit of his sin; Christ wore them as a crown. Adam left the garden to die; Christ was laid in a garden tomb, and rose. And the promise never pictured a victory without cost. He shared our flesh and blood,

speaker: READER
text: so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death

speaker: GUIDE
text: The strike to the heel and the crushing of the head happen in the same act.

chapter: The way to the tree of life
speaker: GUIDE
text: When Jesus died, the veil with its cherubim was torn from top to bottom. Believers now come in

chapter: The way to the tree of life
speaker: READER
text: by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body

chapter: The way to the tree of life
speaker: GUIDE
text: The Bible closes by undoing this chapter. No longer any curse. The tree of life open beside the river. And the pair who hid from God are answered by a people who

chapter: The way to the tree of life
speaker: READER
text: will see His face

chapter: The way to the tree of life
speaker: GUIDE
text: So hear God's questions as grace. Do not hide or blame. Come out and confess, and trust the God who promised a Rescuer and clothed the naked.

chapter: The way to the tree of life
speaker: GUIDE
text: God covered their shame with garments He provided. What are you using to cover your own shame, and what would it mean to receive God's covering in Christ instead?
